text: We have 3 types of designs. Feature designs are the common case, but we also support design systems and shells. Design systems are interesting because we use a design system to build itself and then to present itself to the team. With the team as the audience, it occurred to me that we might do the same thing for presenting the architecture of a project in a way that's understandable to architects and developers and allows an agent to consider architectural choices when implementing designs. Help me plan this and design what it might look like.

1	# Prelude
2	
3	A tool for designing (and later building) apps with an agent: pick a folder,
4	chat with an agent, watch the design appear. The plan, its ground rules and
5	every decision taken are in `docs/plan.md`. Read it before adding a feature.
6	Nothing gets added until we've decided where it fits in the simple model
7	(folder, design, session, screen; a chat surface and a design surface).
8	
9	## Koda
10	
11	This application is built with Koda. Before writing or changing a view, a
12	stylesheet or a handler, load the matching skill - `koda-app-authoring`,
13	`koda-styling`, `koda-server-setup` (and `koda-composition` for anything that
14	crosses an application or a host) - and follow it. Look attributes up in the
15	Koda reference (`node_modules/@kodalang/core/docs/reference.md`, the version
16	Prelude depends on) rather than from memory. Run `koda-review` before calling a
17	change finished.
18	
19	Koda is the npm package `@kodalang/core`, pinned in `package.json`, and it ships
20	its skills. The ones in `.claude/skills/` are copies of the installed package's;
21	`test/skills.test.js` fails when they differ. After upgrading Koda, run
22	`npm run skills` to copy them again, and read what changed.
23	
24	## Working here
25	
26	- `npm start` runs Prelude on http://localhost:4200 (`PORT` to change it).
27	  Views are cached when the server starts: restart it after changing one.
28	- `npm test` runs the tests (node --test). Add tests for what you build.
29	- The desktop app: `npm run build:shell` builds `tauri/src-tauri` (about 10
30	  minutes from cold) into `dist-shell/Prelude.exe`. `npm run test:shell` runs its
31	  Rust tests. The app is a window on the server: it uses one already answering
32	  `/health` on localhost:4200 (`npm start`), or else starts `node start.js`
33	  itself (Prelude's folder is found above the exe, or `--root`/`PRELUDE_ROOT`;
34	  its output goes to `~/.prelude/server.log`) and stops it on quit. `--server

1	# Prelude — plan
2	
3	A tool for designing (and later building) apps with an agent. Built with Koda.
4	It starts as the smallest thing that works: **pick a folder, chat with an agent,
5	watch the design appear.** Features are added only after we've decided where they fit
6	in that model.
7	
8	## The model
9	
10	There are five nouns, and nothing else until a new one earns its place (the fifth, Fix, earned its place in step 11).
11	
12	| Noun | What it is | Where it lives |
13	| --- | --- | --- |
14	| **Project** | What you're designing (and later building), kept in a folder you chose, usually a repo | anywhere on disk |
15	| **Design** | A named body of work (screens + notes) built up over many sessions; usually one feature | `prelude/<design>/` |
16	| **Session** | One conversation with the agent, contributing to one design or one fix | `prelude/<design>/sessions/<id>/` |
17	| **Screen** | One page of the design | `prelude/<design>/screens/NN-name.html` |
18	| **Fix** | One problem in a project, outside any one design, worked on in sessions on a branch of its own | `prelude/fixes/<slug>/` |
19	
20	The interface has two surfaces, modeled on OrchestratR's design session:
21	
22	- **Chat**: the current session's transcript, with filters, the message box, and a
23	  session switcher ("New session" starts another). Any session can be continued on
24	  the machine that started it.
25	- **Design**: the preview, with a screen picker, Refresh, Open in browser and Pop out.
26	
27	Pop out moves the Design surface to its own window, so one window holds the chat and
28	the other holds the design.

1	# Prelude Shell - notes
2	
3	Prelude's own app shell: the layouts Prelude's pages render in. Drafted from
4	what Prelude ships (`server/views/layout.eta`, the `.bar`/`.page`/`.workspace`
5	rules in `server/public/prelude.css`, and the pop-out `_window.eta`), on the
6	Prelude Design System. Gallery: `/gallery` (with `/drawer`, `/modal`,
7	`/notice` over it), `/gallery/workspace`, `/gallery/window`.
8	
9	## Layouts
10	
11	- **app** - the bar, then the page scrolling with the window. Pages hold their
12	  own width (`.center`); the shell gives the room above and below. Projects, a
13	  project, Build.
14	- ~~**workspace**~~ - retired 2026-10-18 (see "One layout for the app's pages"
15	  below). A design's page (chat + surface) is in the app layout and fills the
16	  window by marking itself `.fills`.
17	- **window** - no bar; the page fills the window. The pop-out design surface.
18	
19	Shared parts in `layouts/` (`_head`, `_bar`, `_agents`, `_regions`), since a layout's
20	includes resolve from there. Chrome CSS is `layouts/shell.css`, all in the
21	`host` layer, styling only `.shell-*`. `styles.css` is the gallery's alone.
22	
23	## Decisions
24	
25	- **The gallery shows placeholders, not content** (Prelude's guidance,
26	  2026-10-16): grey `.skeleton` blocks (styles.css) wherever a page or an
27	  overlay puts content, so what's real on screen is the layout's. The only
28	  real content is the buttons that open each region. Placeholder headings keep
29	  a hidden name ("Sample drawer", "Sample question"), so the dialog is still

Here's how I'd shape it. It's a draft, and I've built nothing yet.

## The idea

An architecture design works the way the design system does: **one set of files that agents read, and a gallery that presents them to people.** It would be a fourth kind (`"kind": "architecture"`, one per project). Its sessions shape it with requests like "harvest it from the code" or "we're moving the renderer out of process". The sample data would be Prelude's own architecture, which today sits in `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/plan.md`.

## What it holds (`architecture/`, like the system's `system/`)

- **Overview:** what the app is, the pieces it runs as (server, renderer, shell, hosts), and its **principles**, each with its reason. "The folder is the database" and "views render only in the sandbox" are examples. This plays the part `guidelines.md` plays for the system.
- **Parts:** one file per part, such as `host.js`, `turns.js` or the renderer. Each says what the part is responsible for, what it owns, what it may use, and which files it covers.
- **Decisions:** one record per file (context, decision, consequences), marked proposed, accepted or superseded. Ids are random, as rules' ids are, so branches merge cleanly. Most of these already exist as plan.md's "Decided …" lines.
- **Flows:** a request or job traced through the parts. Examples: a turn, a cold load of an overlay, a POST answered from the working copy.

## The gallery (for architects and developers)

1. **Overview:** a map of the parts and what each uses, plus the principles.
2. **A part:** its responsibility, what uses it and what it uses, the decisions that bind it, and the designs whose pages reach it.
3. **Decisions:** the log, filterable by status and part, with each record opening in a drawer.
4. **A flow:** numbered steps, each naming the part it runs in.

## How agents use it

Design, build and fix sessions read the principles and the parts they touch. When a change would go against them, the agent writes a **proposed decision** instead of drifting quietly, the same way a rule starts as *proposed*. Like a system change, it travels on the branch and gets reviewed there.

## Questions before I build

1. **Source of truth:** should the gallery be views over states that copy the files (possible today, but everything gets written twice), or should Prelude read `architecture/` directly, the way it reads `RULES.md`? I'd go with the second, and design the screens now with states shaped like what Prelude would read.
2. **Format:** markdown with a short header per file (my preference, since it's easy for people and agents to read and edit), or JSON?
3. **Drift:** is a check worth planning now? One example: compare a part's "may use" against the code's imports.
4. **Scope for this session:** should I design the four gallery pages with Prelude as the data? The map needs a diagram component, which I'd add to the design system on this branch.

I've written this proposal and the open questions into `prelude/architecture/NOTES.md`.

I've designed the four pages, with Prelude's own architecture as the data. I couldn't see the preview myself, so nothing has been looked at yet. Prelude's check after this turn will say whether any page fails to render.

**The pages**, at Prelude's own URLs under `/f/:folder/architecture`:
- **Architecture** (the overview): a summary, then a **map** of 19 parts in six layers, each part a link and flagged when the check found something in it. Below the map are the seven principles, each with its reason. Down the side:
  - "Checked against the code";
  - the latest decisions;
  - the flows;
  - "Read by every agent", which says how sessions use the architecture.
- **A part**, such as Design host: what it's responsible for and what isn't its job, the decisions that bind it, and what the check found. Down the side: what it may use, what uses it, what it owns, and its files.
- **Decisions**: search by id or title as you type, and filter to proposed, accepted or superseded. Each decision opens in the drawer with its context, the decision and its consequences. A proposed one also says which branch proposed it, and that merging that branch accepts it.
- **A flow**, such as "A turn": a table of steps, each naming the part it happens in, plus the decisions behind it.

**States**:
- `01-typical`: the check finds two things.
- `02-not-written`: an empty page offering "Draft it from the code…".
- `03-drifted`: five findings, including a use of a part in a layer above and a named file that isn't there.

The event "A turn's check read the code again" refreshes the check card.

**How the check works**: it's planned in `NOTES.md` and appears in the sample as the proposed decision D-r0k. After every turn that changes code, Prelude would:
1. Read the imports of the files that changed.
2. Find each file's part from that part's file list.
3. Report a use the part doesn't say it may make, a file no part names, and a named file that isn't there.

Build and fix agents get the findings with their next message, the same way they get pages that don't render.

**The markdown format**: one file each for the overview, every part, every decision and every flow, in the design's `architecture/` folder. Each file has a short header and fixed sections. The full shape is in `NOTES.md`.

**Design system changes** (on this branch):
- A new **map** component: layers of part boxes, with the labels moving above the parts when narrow. It has its own component file and is on the components screen in the gallery.
- The words "architecture", "part", "decision" and "flow" added to the Words table in the guidelines.

I wrote seven rules, all *proposed*, including that merging a branch accepts its decisions and that agents propose a decision rather than drift. I chose the shown-on state names as `@ 03-drifted`; if that's the wrong form, Prelude will flag it.

Still open, and noted in `NOTES.md`:
- Where the project's own page links to Architecture. That page belongs to Project Landing Page, so I didn't change it.
- Whether a design's page should show the parts its pages reach.
- How the check reads imports in stacks other than JavaScript.

I fixed the two rules Prelude flagged: R-4vx and R-k5e now say `@ drifted`. Since `03-drifted` wasn't recognised, I've assumed Prelude drops the number from state names; its next check will show whether that's right.

**1 and 2:** I've noted in `NOTES.md` that you'll link to Architecture from Project Landing Page. Whether a design's page should show the parts it reaches stays an open question.

**3. Checking imports in other stacks.** My recommendation is small readers built into Prelude, one per language, rather than asking each app's host.

- **Why not the host:** the check has to run where no host is running, such as in CI and with `npm run check`. A host also only starts once you've approved it for that project.
- **What a reader does:** it lists the imports in each file, line by line, with no compiler. What happens next depends on the language:
  - **Imports that name a file** (JavaScript and TypeScript, Python, Go, Ruby, PHP): the reader finds the imported file, and from that the part that lists it.
  - **Imports that name a namespace** (C#, Java, Kotlin): a part's file also says which namespaces it holds, for example `names: Spark.Servicing.*`. Each `using` or `import` is matched to the part holding that namespace. For .NET, each `.csproj`'s project references get the same treatment, as a rougher check of uses.
  - **A language with no reader:** files are still checked for belonging to a part and for existing, but uses aren't checked, and the check says so once.
- **If a reader is too rough:** add an endpoint to the host contract that gives exact imports. I'd only do this once a real project needs it.

This is in `NOTES.md` as recommended but not yet agreed, with the choice between readers and the host left as an open question.
